content:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: BrightLedger x Redwood — security / compliance review (SSO, audit logs, SOC2)
Date: 2025-02-18
Time: 1:00pm–1:37pm PT
Duration: 37 min

Attendees
- Stephanie Nguyen (Redwood, AE)
- Markus Klein (Redwood, Solutions Engineering)
- Naomi Feldman (Redwood, Security/Compliance Product)
- David Kim (Redwood, Biz Systems/HubSpot admin) (joined late)
- Sonia Patel (BrightLedger, Security & Compliance)
- Eric Huang (BrightLedger, Eng Manager)
- Linda Reyes (BrightLedger, Procurement)
- Matt Kline (BrightLedger, IT)

Summary (auto)
BrightLedger requested a security and compliance review driven by internal vendor onboarding requirements. They asked for SOC 2 Type II, SSO/SAML support, audit logs (access + admin activity), encryption/KMS posture, data retention, and subprocessor details. Redwood clarified current controls for Hosted and Dedicated, and discussed when Redwood Private (VPC) is recommended for regulated workloads and network isolation. Procurement timeline: BrightLedger aims to complete security review in ~2–3 weeks to align with an internal pilot expansion.

Topics (auto)
- SOC 2 / compliance scope and evidence
- SSO / SAML and RBAC
- Audit logs: what events, retention, export
- Data handling: prompts/outputs retention, training usage, encryption
- Deployment options: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC)
- Procurement timeline and next steps

Questions (auto)
- Does Redwood have SOC 2 Type II? What’s the report period and scope?
- Is SAML required for both Console and API access? Is SCIM supported?
- What audit log events are available (login, key creation, model changes, org settings)?
- Can we get data residency (EU/US) and private networking?
- How long do you retain request/response data and logs? Can it be configured?

Transcript

[00:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Alright, I think we’re all here. Sonia, Eric, Linda, Matt—good to meet you all. I’m Stephanie, I work with the commercial side. I’ve got Markus on the line, he’s our solutions engineer, and Naomi who owns security and compliance product. The goal today is basically just go through your checklist and figure out what’s gating you.

[00:18] Sonia Patel: Yep, thanks Stephanie. So, short version: we’re already using your hosted API in dev, but to move this into production our vendor onboarding requires SOC 2 Type II, SSO, audit logs, and a couple data handling attestations.

[00:31] Eric Huang: And ideally we don’t want to slow down the pilot. We’re trying to keep engineering moving while security does their thing.

[00:38] Markus Klein: Makes sense. We’ll try to be crisp. Also, if we need to follow up with docs under NDA we can do that right after.

[00:46] Stephanie Nguyen: Yep. Also just to level set—this call got triggered because your team requested access to some of our security docs in the console and pricing pages. So this is exactly the right step. We’re treating it as a security review, not a sales pitch.

[01:01] Sonia Patel: Great. I’ll be direct then. Do you have a SOC 2 Type II report we can review? Not just “in progress.”

[01:08] Naomi Feldman: Yes. Redwood has an active SOC 2 Type II. It covers Security and Availability criteria. We can share the report under NDA. The report period is last year’s full cycle—so it’s not like a one-month stub.

[01:24] Linda Reyes: Under NDA is fine, we have a standard mutual NDA for vendors. We’ll need the report plus your subprocessor list and DPA language.

[01:33] Naomi Feldman: We have a subprocessor page and we can provide the list as part of the security pack. DPA is available. We also have a standard set of security FAQs that answer the “do you train on our data” question.

[01:47] Sonia Patel: Okay good. Next: SSO. Do you support SAML, and for what surfaces? We have a policy that console access must use SSO. API keys are separate but should be managed.

[01:59] Naomi Feldman: Yes, we support SSO via SAML for the Redwood Console for enterprise plans. RBAC is role-based within the org. For API access, it’s still API keys / service tokens—those are managed in the console, so the console SSO is usually what customers require.

[02:17] Matt Kline: When you say “enterprise plans,” that means Dedicated or Private, right? Or can we do it with hosted while we ramp?

[02:26] Stephanie Nguyen: Typically SSO is bundled with Dedicated and Private. We can talk about timing—some customers start hosted and then flip SSO on as they move to a commit. But we can align it to your rollout.

[02:39] Sonia Patel: Is SCIM supported? We prefer automated provisioning, not manual.

[02:45] Naomi Feldman: SCIM is not generally available for all tenants today. Some customers do manual provisioning with SSO enforced and tight admin roles. If SCIM is a hard requirement for production go-live we need to confirm your timing and whether we can accommodate.

[03:01] Eric Huang: For us, SAML is the minimum. SCIM is “nice to have” unless security says otherwise.

[03:08] Sonia Patel: I’ll note that. Next: audit logs. What do you log? Specifically: authentication events, admin changes, API key creation, model routing changes, and access to data.

[03:22] Markus Klein: Great question. We have audit logs for org-level admin actions in the console—like user role changes, key creation, changes to quotas, and certain configuration changes. For the API side, there are request logs and usage metrics, but we’re careful about PII.

[03:38] Sonia Patel: That’s vague. I need specifics. Like, do you log “user X downloaded invoice” or “user X created a key” and can I export it?

[03:47] Naomi Feldman: For export: yes, we can provide an export mechanism depending on tier—either API access to audit events or scheduled exports. On “user X”—we log the actor identifier at the account level, but we avoid leaking customer end-user PII. The actor is your org user.

[04:05] Sonia Patel: Right. I’m not asking for our customers’ PII, I’m asking for our admin users.

[04:10] Naomi Feldman: Yep. Admin actor attribution is supported.

[04:14] Linda Reyes: What’s retention on audit logs?

[04:18] Naomi Feldman: Default retention varies by plan. For enterprise we can do extended retention. We can also align to your requirements—like 90 days or 1 year. There are tradeoffs on storage and cost.

[04:32] Matt Kline: Also, do you integrate with a SIEM? Splunk, Datadog, whatever.

[04:37] Markus Klein: We don’t have a one-click “send to Splunk” for every customer, but we provide export endpoints and webhook-ish patterns that customers use to pipe to their SIEM. We can share examples.

[04:51] Sonia Patel: Okay. Next: data handling. Do you train on prompts and outputs? Do you store them? And how do you encrypt them?

[05:00] Naomi Feldman: Redwood does not train foundation models on customer prompts/outputs. For retention: by default we retain limited request metadata for abuse monitoring and debugging, but we can configure reduced retention for enterprise. On encryption: data is encrypted in transit (TLS) and at rest. For Private deployments we can use customer-managed keys depending on environment.

[05:23] Eric Huang: When you say “request metadata,” is it like token counts and latency? Or actual prompt text?

[05:29] Markus Klein: It depends. For hosted, some customers allow short-term retention of prompt/response for debugging; others choose “no content retention” mode. We do have controls there. We can walk through what’s available for your tier.

[05:42] Sonia Patel: We require no content retention in production unless there is a documented exception.

[05:47] Stephanie Nguyen: Totally understood. That’s common. We’ll confirm the exact configuration and put it in writing.

[05:55] Linda Reyes: We also need data residency. Are you able to keep data in the US only? We have some EU customers as well.

[06:03] Markus Klein: We can route by region. For Dedicated we can place capacity in specific regions; for Private it’s in your VPC so you choose the region. If you need strict “EU only,” Lukas on our side handles EMEA but the capability exists—just depends on deployment option.

[06:21] Sonia Patel: We probably start US-only. EU later.

[06:25] Eric Huang: The bigger question is whether hosted is okay for production. Our platform team is pushing for VPC.

[06:33] Markus Klein: That usually comes down to network isolation requirements. If you need private networking, static egress, VPC endpoints, then Private is the fit. Dedicated is “isolated capacity” but still managed by us—private networking is more limited.

[06:48] Sonia Patel: Our policy says: for systems that process PII we prefer VPC or on-prem. But this is model inference—prompts can include customer data, so yes, it can be PII.

[07:00] Naomi Feldman: Understood. Many customers treat it that way. The most straightforward answer is Redwood Private in a customer VPC with customer-managed networking controls. If you’re earlier-stage, sometimes teams do hosted for dev and then move to Private for prod.

[07:17] Stephanie Nguyen: From a procurement standpoint, we can also align it. You don’t have to decide everything today, but we do need to know what your “go-live” policy requires.

[07:27] Sonia Patel: Okay, let me get more tactical. SSO/SAML: required. Audit logs: required. SOC2 Type II: required. Data retention: must be configurable to “no content retention.” VPC: strongly preferred. What can you meet in the next 30 days?

[07:44] Markus Klein: Within 30 days: SOC2 report under NDA, SAML for Console on enterprise plan, audit logs with export, and reduced/no content retention settings—those are all workable. VPC: Redwood Private can be provisioned on that timeline, but there’s some setup: networking, IAM, and a short readiness review.

[08:06] Matt Kline: Does Private mean we manage the GPUs?

[08:09] Markus Klein: No, we can do managed Private where we operate the service in your VPC, depending on the model. You control network and access boundaries; we manage the runtime and updates under an agreed process.

[08:24] Sonia Patel: And does your staff have access into our VPC?

[08:27] Naomi Feldman: Access is controlled and audited. It’s typically break-glass with approvals and logging. We can go through the support access model. Some customers require that support sessions are only initiated by customer and time-bound.

[08:44] Eric Huang: This is similar to other vendors we use.

[08:47] Sonia Patel: Okay. Another question: do you support customer-managed keys, like KMS? We use AWS KMS.

[08:54] Naomi Feldman: For Private deployments, yes, we can integrate with KMS for encryption at rest. For hosted, it’s Redwood-managed keys but still encrypted at rest.

[09:06] Linda Reyes: Can you provide a list of subprocessors? Especially anything that would see content.

[09:11] Naomi Feldman: Yes. Subprocessors are listed, and we can clarify which ones process what. Content processing is limited and controlled by retention settings. We’ll provide that in the packet.

[09:24] Sonia Patel: We also have to ask: do you use any third-party model provider underneath? Like do you forward to OpenAI or Anthropic?

[09:32] Markus Klein: For the models you’re using with us today, it’s served on our infrastructure. We don’t proxy your request to OpenAI or Anthropic. We do support routing policies across model variants within Redwood, but it’s our hosted runtime.

[09:48] Eric Huang: That’s important. We had concerns with Bedrock style “who is the subprocessor.”

[09:54] Sonia Patel: Good. Can you commit contractually that you don’t train on our data and don’t share it with other customers?

[10:02] Stephanie Nguyen: Yes, that’s in our standard terms and DPA. Naomi can confirm details but yes.

[10:09] Naomi Feldman: Correct. We can provide the language and map it to your questionnaire.

[10:15] Sonia Patel: Great. Now, audit logs again—do you log API access events? We need something like “token used” or “key used” and basic metadata.

[10:25] Markus Klein: We provide per-key usage analytics—counts, latency, error codes, and timestamps. For “who used it,” API keys are not tied to an individual user unless you structure it that way. Most customers rotate keys and tag them by service.

[10:42] Matt Kline: Do you have IP allowlisting?

[10:45] Markus Klein: For Private, you can do that at the network layer. For hosted, we have some controls but not full IP allowlisting for all tenants. We can check what’s available on your plan.

[10:58] Sonia Patel: For production, we’d want Private then.

[11:01] Stephanie Nguyen: That’s consistent with what you said earlier.

[11:06] Linda Reyes: I need to understand pricing implications. Are we talking like a big jump from hosted usage-based?

[11:12] Stephanie Nguyen: Private and Dedicated are contract-based. It’s typically a commit. The reason teams do it is for predictable capacity and security controls (SSO, audit logs, private networking). I can send a range after we confirm scope—like throughput and region.

[11:28] Eric Huang: We also have a timing problem: engineering wants to keep building now on hosted. Security wants to approve before production. Can we do a staged approach?

[11:38] Markus Klein: Absolutely. Common approach: dev/staging on hosted; production on Private once approved. We can keep API compatibility so you don’t rewrite.

[11:49] Sonia Patel: That helps. I just need to ensure the hosted environment doesn’t inadvertently store content while we’re testing. Even in dev, we’d prefer minimal retention.

[12:00] Naomi Feldman: We can set your org’s retention mode. If you’re okay, we can enforce “no content retention” across environments. There may be tradeoffs in supportability, but it’s doable.

[12:13] Eric Huang: I’m okay with that if we can still debug. We can add our own logging.

[12:19] Markus Klein: Yeah, we can share best practices—like structured output logging on your side without sending prompts back to us.

[12:27] Sonia Patel: Okay. Switching gears: do you have ISO 27001? Our policy asks, but SOC2 Type II is usually acceptable.

[12:34] Naomi Feldman: We do not lead with ISO today. SOC2 Type II is our primary attestation. If ISO is a hard requirement, we should flag it early. Most US-based procurement accepts SOC2.

[12:47] Linda Reyes: It’s not hard requirement. We just tick the box.

[12:50] Sonia Patel: Another question: do you have penetration test results you can share?

[12:55] Naomi Feldman: We can share a pen test summary and remediation statement, typically not raw findings, again under NDA.

[13:06] Matt Kline: And vulnerability management? Do you have a bug bounty?

[13:10] Naomi Feldman: Yes, we have a vulnerability disclosure process and routine scanning. Bug bounty is limited scope but we can provide the policy.

[13:19] Eric Huang: Also, from engineering: do you support SSO for API access? Like OAuth or something.

[13:25] Markus Klein: Not for API requests today. It’s token-based. SSO is for the Console and admin operations. Most teams treat API keys as service credentials and store them in their secret manager.

[13:39] Sonia Patel: That’s acceptable.

[13:41] Stephanie Nguyen: Linda, on procurement timeline—what are we aiming for? Just so we can match our internal steps.

[13:47] Linda Reyes: Best case: security review completed in two weeks, vendor onboarding in the third week, and then we issue a PO or sign order form. But it depends on how fast we get evidence. If we don’t get the SOC2 in time, it slips.

[14:07] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay. We can move quickly once NDA is signed. I’ll send NDA today.

[14:13] Sonia Patel: We already have an NDA template. I’ll send it to you.

[14:16] Stephanie Nguyen: Perfect.

[14:19] Markus Klein: Sonia, do you have a questionnaire you want us to fill out, or are you doing a doc review?

[14:25] Sonia Patel: We have a questionnaire. It’s not crazy but it’s like 80 questions. Some sections: access control, incident response, BCP, encryption, data deletion.

[14:36] Naomi Feldman: Great. Send it over; we’ll map it to our controls and provide evidence pointers.

[14:43] Eric Huang: Data deletion is important. If we send prompts, can we request deletion?

[14:49] Naomi Feldman: Yes. For enterprise, we can support deletion requests consistent with retention settings. If you run in “no content retention,” there’s very little content to delete. Logs still exist but they don’t contain prompt content.

[15:07] Sonia Patel: What about support tickets? Sometimes vendors ask for sample prompts to debug. We can’t do that.

[15:13] Markus Klein: Understood. We can operate with synthetic prompts and metadata. Our support process can be configured so we don’t ask for content. We’ll document that.

[15:24] Sonia Patel: Great.

[15:26] (crosstalk) Eric Huang: Also, we saw something about “audit logs” in your docs but it didn’t say export.

[15:31] Markus Klein: Yeah, the doc is a bit behind. We have internal copy updates in flight. We’ll send a more precise list of events and export method.

[15:42] Sonia Patel: Please do. Otherwise procurement will block.

[15:45] Stephanie Nguyen: Noted.

[15:48] David Kim: Hey all—sorry, jumping in late. David Kim here, I run our HubSpot and some of the admin tooling. I’m here mostly to listen if there are questions about identity or provisioning.

[16:00] Sonia Patel: Hi David. Identity question: SAML—do you support Okta?

[16:05] David Kim: Yes, Okta is supported. We have setup guides for Okta and Azure AD. It’s standard SAML 2.0.

[16:14] Sonia Patel: And can you enforce it, so no password logins?

[16:18] David Kim: Yes, you can enforce SSO required for the org.

[16:22] Matt Kline: Any MFA requirements?

[16:24] David Kim: With SSO, MFA is handled by your IdP. For non-SSO flows, we have MFA options but again—enterprise tends to enforce SSO.

[16:36] Sonia Patel: Great. RBAC: can we separate billing admin from security admin?

[16:41] David Kim: We have roles—admin vs developer vs viewer, and some granular permissions. If you need a specific separation of duties, tell us what exact roles you want; we can confirm.

[16:54] Naomi Feldman: We also have an audit log entry for role changes, which usually satisfies SoD controls.

[17:02] Sonia Patel: Okay.

[17:04] Eric Huang: Another policy we have is incident notification. What’s your incident response? Do you have an SLA to notify within X hours?

[17:12] Naomi Feldman: We have an incident response program. Contractually, we can agree to notification timelines for security incidents. Typical is within 72 hours of confirmation, sometimes faster depending on severity. We can align to your requirement.

[17:27] Linda Reyes: Our template says 48 hours.

[17:30] Stephanie Nguyen: We’ll review and revert. Usually workable.

[17:34] Sonia Patel: Also, do you have a public status page?

[17:37] Markus Klein: Yes, we have a status page and we can provide uptime history. For Dedicated/Private, SLAs are different.

[17:46] Sonia Patel: Okay.

[17:48] Markus Klein: Can I ask one question back? What’s driving the move from hosted to Private—just policy, or do you also have throughput/latency requirements?

[17:58] Eric Huang: Both. We’re seeing concurrency spikes at end-of-month reporting. We also hit rate limits a couple times. But security is the forcing function.

[18:07] Stephanie Nguyen: That matches what we’ve seen—your usage is growing and you’ve had some 429s. That’s partly why we thought Dedicated/Private could help.

[18:17] Sonia Patel: Let’s keep it on security today.

[18:19] Stephanie Nguyen: Fair.

[18:22] Sonia Patel: Any compliance with GDPR? We have EU users.

[18:26] Naomi Feldman: We support GDPR requirements via DPA, deletion, and data handling controls. Data residency is an architectural question—if you need EU-only processing, we’d recommend deploying EU region capacity or Private.

[18:43] Sonia Patel: Okay.

[18:45] Matt Kline: For Private, do you support logging into our CloudWatch? Like export logs into our account.

[18:51] Markus Klein: For Private, since it’s in your VPC, yes, you can integrate with your logging stack. We can forward audit events / system logs into CloudWatch or your SIEM depending on architecture.

[19:06] Sonia Patel: That’s good.

[19:08] Linda Reyes: I want to confirm what we’ll receive after this call. I need a list so I can track.

[19:13] Stephanie Nguyen: Yep. You’ll get: NDA, SOC2 report after NDA, security pack (subprocessors, pen test summary, DPA), and an audit log events list + retention options. Also, Naomi will take your questionnaire.

[19:29] Sonia Patel: Great.

[19:31] Eric Huang: Can you answer whether you have any government certifications? FedRAMP?

[19:37] Naomi Feldman: We are not FedRAMP authorized today.

[19:41] Sonia Patel: Okay, not required.

[19:44] Markus Klein: Sonia, one more on audit logs—do you need “read access” events? Like who viewed logs or who viewed usage dashboards?

[19:53] Sonia Patel: Preferably yes. At minimum, admin changes. Read access is good but not always required. Our auditors sometimes ask.

[20:04] Naomi Feldman: We’ll document what we have today and what’s on roadmap. I don’t want to overpromise.

[20:10] Sonia Patel: Thank you.

[20:12] Stephanie Nguyen: Anything else gating procurement? Sometimes legal asks about limitation of liability or data processing terms.

[20:19] Linda Reyes: Yeah, legal will review. But the long pole is evidence for SOC2 and the data retention / no training commitments.

[20:29] Stephanie Nguyen: Understood.

[20:31] Sonia Patel: One more—do you use any subcontractors for support that could access our account? Like offshore support.

[20:38] Naomi Feldman: Support is primarily in-house. Any subprocessors are disclosed. Access is role-based and logged. We can answer in the questionnaire.

[20:50] Sonia Patel: Great.

[20:52] Markus Klein: Since you mentioned rate limits earlier—if you move to Dedicated/Private, you’ll have predictable throughput and we can set explicit quotas and burst policies. But again, we’ll keep it separate.

[21:03] Eric Huang: Noted.

[21:05] Sonia Patel: Okay, timeline. I’ll send the questionnaire by tomorrow. Can you turn it around quickly?

[21:11] Naomi Feldman: Yes, if we get it tomorrow, we can aim for initial responses within 2 business days, and then any follow-ups.

[21:19] Linda Reyes: And NDA—if we send ours today, can you sign it quickly?

[21:23] Stephanie Nguyen: Yes, I’ll route it today.

[21:27] David Kim: If you need SSO setup docs, tell me your IdP (Okta) and I’ll send the exact guide.

[21:33] Matt Kline: Okta.

[21:35] David Kim: Great.

[21:37] Sonia Patel: Anything else you need from us?

[21:40] Markus Klein: It would help to know whether “Private in VPC” is mandatory for production go-live, or if Dedicated is acceptable with strong controls.

[21:49] Sonia Patel: I think policy says VPC preferred. But I can check if Dedicated with SSO + audit logs is acceptable for phase 1.

[21:58] Stephanie Nguyen: That would be helpful, because it affects what we propose.

[22:03] Eric Huang: Engineering would prefer not to manage VPC stuff if possible, but we can if required.

[22:10] Markus Klein: We can handle a lot of the heavy lifting; you’d mainly provide networking requirements.

[22:16] Sonia Patel: Okay.

[22:18] Stephanie Nguyen: Last thing—competitor comparisons sometimes come up in procurement. Are you evaluating other providers?

[22:24] Linda Reyes: The business is looking at Bedrock and OpenAI direct. Engineering likes you because of performance and model options.

[22:33] Sonia Patel: From security, we just care that controls are there.

[22:37] Stephanie Nguyen: Totally. We’ll focus on that.

[22:41] Naomi Feldman: Sonia, before we wrap, any red flags you’ve seen in our docs so far? Sometimes there’s wording that’s confusing.

[22:48] Sonia Patel: The docs about retention and audit logs are unclear. It reads like you might store content by default.

[22:55] Naomi Feldman: Thanks. We’ll follow up with precise language: what’s default, what can be configured, and what we commit to contractually.

[23:06] Sonia Patel: Great.

[23:08] Stephanie Nguyen: Alright, let’s do quick recap and next steps.

[23:12] Stephanie Nguyen: I’ll send NDA and coordinate SOC2 report share. Naomi will take the questionnaire and send the security pack. Markus will send the audit log events list and retention/export options. David will send Okta SAML setup guide. Sonia you’ll send your questionnaire and NDA template. Linda you’ll keep us honest on timeline.

[23:34] Linda Reyes: Yes.

[23:35] Sonia Patel: Yep.

[23:36] Eric Huang: Sounds good.

[23:38] Stephanie Nguyen: Perfect. Thanks everyone.

[23:41] (meeting ended)

Notes
- Several portions had crosstalk; speaker attribution may be imperfect.
- Redwood referenced the call being triggered by recent security/SSO doc engagement (“security intent” signal) and ongoing self-serve usage.
